case_name: Nayyar v. Manufacturers Life Insurance Company
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Nayyar v. Manufacturers Life Insurance
Company,

2016 BCSC 1587

Date: 20160829

Docket:
S161695

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Annu
Radha Nayyar and Sanjay Nayyar et al

Plaintiffs

And

Manufacturers Life Insurance Company/La Compagnie D’Assurance Vie
Manufacturers Carrying on Business as Manulife Financial and Costco Wholesale
Canada Ltd.

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Voith

Reasons for Judgment

Appearing on their own behalf:

Annu
Radha Nayyar

and Sanjay Nayyar

Counsel for the Defendant, Manufacturers
Life Insurance Company, carrying on business as Manulife Financial:

Bert
Terzian

Counsel for the Defendant, Costco Wholesale
Canada Ltd.

Herman
Van Ommen, Q.C.

Gord Lamb A/S

Place and Date of Trial/Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

July
4, 2016

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

August
29, 2016

[
1
]

The applicants/defendants, Manufacturers Life
Insurance Company (“Manulife”) and Costco Wholesale Canada Ltd. (“Costco”) seek
two orders:

i)          that
the plaintiffs current action be struck out as frivolous, vexatious, and an
abuse of the court’s process pursuant to Rules 9-5(1)(a) and (d) of the
Supreme
Civil Court Rules
,
B.C. Reg. 168/2009
[
Rules
]; and

ii)         that
the plaintiffs, Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar, be declared vexatious litigants,
preventing them from instituting any legal proceedings against Costco or
Manulife, and any related entities, and their directors, officers, employees,
and agents without leave of the court.

Overview and Background

[
2
]

The history that underlies the present dispute
is, I am satisfied, concisely and accurately described in Costco’s notice of application.
Indeed, the plaintiffs do not, in any meaningful way, contest that chronology.
In addition, that history is supported by various objective materials including
correspondence, court records, court orders, and judgments of both this Court
and the Court of Appeal. Accordingly, I have relied on that chronology
extensively.

[
3
]

The plaintiff, Mrs. Nayyar, is a former
employee of Costco. Pursuant to Mrs. Nayyar’s contract of employment,
Costco provided her with group benefits, including short-term and long-term
disability benefits (the “Plan”). Manulife administered the Plan under an
administrative services contract with Costco for short-term disability claims,
and for the first 24 months of Mrs. Nayyar’s long-term disability claims,
Costco was the insurer and Manulife administered the Plan. Thereafter, Manulife
was the insurer and administered its own disability insurance policy.

[
4
]

In 2004, Mrs. Nayyar filed a claim against
Manulife and Costco for disability benefits (the “Benefits Claim”). In this
action, Mrs. Nayyar also advanced numerous allegations of bad faith
against the defendants for their alleged conduct in the course of managing and
adjudicating her claims for benefits. Mrs. Nayyar also made serious
allegations of misconduct against the defendants’ counsel in relation to their
conduct of the litigation.

[
5
]

Justice Walker oversaw the case management of
this action. In October 2010, Walker J. severed and stayed the bad faith claim
pending determination of Mrs. Nayyar’s contractual entitlement to
disability benefits.

[
6
]

For most of the litigation, Mrs. Nayyar was
self-represented and her husband purported to act as her litigation agent. He
provided her with considerable direction and assistance. Indeed, a consistent
theme in the various sets of reasons that followed thereafter was that it was Mr. Nayyar
who drove and oversaw the litigation.

[
7
]

In October 2010, the defendants brought a motion
to prevent Mr. Nayyar from acting on Mrs. Nayyar’s behalf. Justice
Walker granted that application. In his oral reasons he determined, among other
things, that Mr. Nayyar could not act as an impartial advocate, that his
judgment was “clouded”, and that he had misrepresented facts to the Court,
though Walker J. did not conclude that those misrepresentations were
intentional;
Nayyar v. Manufacturers Life Insurance Company
,
2010 BCSC
1671
at paras.
8
, 15 [
Nayyar
2010].

[
8
]

Even after his removal as litigation agent in
the action, Mr. Nayyar continued to direct that action. He remained the
point of contact for Mrs. Nayyar. He signed court documents and he
insisted on communicating on her behalf with counsel and with the Registry.

[
9
]

The applicants argue, and the relevant exhibits
establish, that Mr. Nayyar’s conduct throughout the litigation was often
intemperate and abusive. He made unfounded accusations against counsel for the
defendants. He used derogatory language in his communications. Aspects of those
communications were threatening to counsel.

[
10
]

In March 2011, Mrs. Nayyar failed to comply
with various court orders, and Mr. Nayyar was cautioned by Walker J. not
to be complicit in or to direct his wife to flaunt the court’s orders. After
addressing Mrs. Nayyar, Walker J. said:

[117]    Mr. Nayyar, you are in the
back of the courtroom. Would you stand up? I see from some of the documents
that you have had a hand in the events that have led up to this application. I
hope you’ve listened to what I have had to say in the courtroom today. You are
not permitted to encourage your wife to breach court orders. Do you understand?

[118]    MR. NAYYAR: Yes, My Lord.

[119]    THE
COURT: I do not want to hear any further applications arising from situations
where you have actively participated in your wife’s failure to comply with
court orders, or where you encouraged your wife not to comply with them. Court
orders may not be disobeyed simply because you have decided that there are
further matters that need to be tended to. Do you understand?

[
11
]

Justice Walker also made a $500 cost award that
was payable in any event of the cause;
Nayyar v. Manufacturers Life
Insurance Company
(03 March 2011), Vancouver S043024, at para. 46
(B.C.S.C.).

[
12
]

Costco’s notice of application refers to the
court having made several special cost awards against Mrs. Nayyar prior to
trial that, in combination, totalled approximately $13,000. There are at least
two such special cost orders, in the application record, that were made by
Walker J. on April 8, 2011 and March 20, 2012, respectively. A further cost
order, in the amount of $12,500, payable to Costco and $250 payable to Manulife,
was made on April 27, 2011.

[
13
]

Justice Walker ultimately granted judgment in
favour of Mrs. Nayyar in the action. Those reasons are indexed at
2012
BCSC 28
. For present purposes, it is noteworthy that in that judgment Walker J.
observed, at para. 58, that Mr. Nayyar was “so consumed with the minutiae
of his wife’s case” that he had difficulty separating fact from argument, and
that his “obsession…caused him to impede the orderly progress of the…action”.

[
14
]

The Court of Appeal set aside the trial judgment
and dismissed Mrs. Nayyar’s claim;
Nayyar v. Costco Wholesale Canada
Ltd.
,
2012 BCCA 501
. In the Court’s reasons, Newbury J.A., at para. 5,
observed that Mrs. Nayyar was “unable to make her case or to answer any
questions from the Court except on her husband’s instruction…”. This conclusion
aligns with my own observations in the hearings that I have overseen.

[
15
]

Following the appeal, Mrs. Nayyar was
ordered to pay substantial costs awards to both Costco and Manulife, and to
repay the funds that Costco had paid her on account of the judgment rendered at
trial;
Nayyar v. Costco Wholesale Canada Ltd.
,
2013 BCCA 107
. The costs
awarded in favour of Costco totalled $185,621.38 and the judgment monies she
was ordered to repay Costco totalled $18,506.23. The costs award in favour of Manulife
totalled $98,832.57.

[
16
]

Mrs. Nayyar did not pay these amounts to
Costco and/or Manulife. Costco and Manulife registered these various sums, and
other special costs awards that had been made against Mrs. Nayyar
(collectively the “Judgment Debts”) against title to certain property (the
“Property”), that was registered solely in the name of Mrs. Nayyar. The
applicants were also able to recover a portion of the Judgment Debts by way of
a series of garnishing orders.

[
17
]

Costco and Manulife commenced proceedings under
the
Court Order Enforcement Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 78 (the
“Execution Proceedings”). On May 13, 2014, the parties appeared before this
Court for a hearing as to the title of the Property. Registrar Cameron
delivered a report which concluded that title to the Property was held by Mrs. Nayyar
alone. It is relevant and important for present purposes that Mr. Nayyar
attended these proceedings and raised no argument in relation to Registrar
Cameron’s findings.

[
18
]

On May 27, 2014, Registrar Cameron’s report on
title was confirmed by the order of Master Taylor, who also granted an order of
sale.

[
19
]

On November 19, 2014, Romilly J. made an order
approving the sale of Mrs. Nayyar’s home. He further ordered that those sales
proceeds be paid into court.

[
20
]

On March 25, 2015, Ehrcke J. ordered the balance
of the sale proceeds be paid out of court in full settlement of the Judgment
Debts owed to Costco, and in partial payment of the Judgment Debts in favour of
Manulife.

[
21
]

Mrs. Nayyar did not take any steps to
appeal any of the orders that I have referred to within the time limits
prescribed by the
Rules
. Furthermore, Mr. Nayyar was aware of the Execution
Proceedings throughout and never, in his own right, advanced any objection to
the relief being sought.

The Nayyars’ Attempts to Re-Litigate

[
22
]

In July 2015, Mrs. Nayyar attempted to have
a case management judge appointed, notwithstanding the fact that the
proceedings between the parties were concluded. Subsequently, Mrs. Nayyar
applied to the court for an acknowledgment of payment. However, the document
advanced by the Nayyars was not an acknowledgment of payment. Instead, it was a
form of agreement that would have had Costco and Manulife pay Mrs. Nayyar
the sum of $99 million. Justice Loo dismissed Mrs. Nayyar’s application
and ordered $250 in costs against her.

[
23
]

On August 20, 2015, nearly four months after the
expiry of the 30-day period to appeal or to seek leave to appeal Ehrcke J.’s
order, Mrs. Nayyar filed an application for leave to appeal and sought an
order from the Court of Appeal requiring Costco and Manulife to sign the
purported acknowledgment of payment. Mr. Nayyar appeared on the
application and made submissions on Mrs. Nayyar’s behalf.

[
24
]

In her oral reasons for judgment, found at
Costco
Wholesale Canada Ltd. v. Nayyar
(31 August 2015) Vancouver CA43028 at
paras. 16-18, 21 (B.C.C.A.), Garson J.A. concluded:

a)         it
appeared that Mrs. Nayyar’s appeal was predicated on an attempt to force
Costco and Manulife to sign an agreement to pay her $99 million;

b)         there
was no apparent legal basis for such a liability;

c)         Mrs. Nayyar’s
actions constitute an attempt to challenge the Court of Appeal’s judgment
dismissing her claims for entitlement to disability benefits; and

d)         there was no merit to Mrs. Nayyar’s appeal.

[
25
]

Justice Garson also said:

[22]      On that basis I think that Ms. Nayyar’s
conduct could be considered an abuse of the Court’s process. It was a wrongful
attempt to seek the Court’s assistance to do that which she is not entitled to
do.

[23]      With some reluctance I award
Costco special costs for today’s hearing.

[24]      Ms. Nayyar,
I might say too, you were unsuccessful in the Court of Appeal and it is not
helpful to you to keep trying to keep this case alive. It is costly to you.

[
26
]

The cost order made by Garson J.A. has not been
paid. It is also noteworthy that there is no suggestion in the reasons of
Garson J.A. that Mr. Nayyar attempted to challenge the order of Ehrcke J. on
the basis that he held a one-half interest in the Property – this being the
primary issue that he now appears to be trying to raise.

[
27
]

Two weeks after Mrs. Nayyar’s appeal was
dismissed, and in response to a demand for payment of the special costs that
had been ordered, Mrs. Nayyar reiterated her demand that Costco sign the
acknowledgment of payment and pay the $99 million figure.

[
28
]

Subsequently, on October 13, 2015, Mrs. Nayyar
filed a petition against Costco and Manulife seeking judicial review (the “Judicial
Review Petition”), in which she again attempted to re-litigate both the
dismissal of the Benefits Claim and the Execution Proceedings, and she sought
to have the respondents sign an agreement to pay her $99 million.

[
29
]

At the same time, Mrs. Nayyar filed another
identical application to the Judicial Review Petition, seeking the same orders
and relief, but under the petition that had been filed by Costco and Manulife in
the
Execution Proceedings
.

[
30
]

I heard the Judicial Review Petition, and the
parallel application that had been filed, on December 7 and 8, 2015. Those
materials raised numerous issues. They re-asserted the merits of the Benefits
Claim. They argued in favour of receiving an acknowledgment of payment (which,
in turn, contemplated the $99 million payment), and they questioned the
legitimacy of the
Execution Proceedings
arguing,
inter alia
, that Mr. Nayyar
had not been served with the original application materials and that his
beneficial interest in the Property had not been recognized. They further
argued that,
inter alia,
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
Part I of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, being Schedule B to the
Canada
Act 1982
(U.K.), 1982, c. 11
,
and the
Class Proceedings Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 50 had relevance. It was Mr. Nayyar who spoke to
virtually the whole of the application.

[
31
]

Over the course of the application, and as Mr. Nayyar
addressed each issue individually, I explained the many and varied difficulties
that the application faced. In particular, I explained that Mrs. Nayyar’s Benefits
Claim against Costco and Manulife had been dismissed, that the Execution
Proceedings had been completed, that these matters could not be revived, and that
the Judicial Review Petition was a further attempt to advance the same or
similar arguments as had been addressed by the Court of Appeal on two earlier
occasions.

[
32
]

Initially, Costco, in light of the history of
the matter, sought another special costs order. Ultimately, the Judicial Review
Petition and the identical application were dismissed by consent. The Nayyars
expressly and unequivocally represented to the Court and to Costco and Manulife
that in exchange for a consent dismissal order without costs, they would not
bring any further claims which revisited these same issues. During the
application, I also confirmed that I would remain seized of the matter in the
event that the Nayyars brought any subsequent applications or actions.

[
33
]

Almost immediately following the dismissal of
the Judicial Review Petition and its mirror application, Mr. Nayyar again began
to advance or reiterate his demands for compensation. On December 15, 2015, he
wrote to Costco asking the company to settle his alleged claim. He alleged that
he had an undeclared interest in the Property that had been sold as part of the

Execution Proceedings
.

[
34
]

On December 21, 2015, Mr. Nayyar again
wrote demanding that Costco and Manulife pay $99 million in damages or that he
would commence an action against both parties.

[
35
]

On January 27, 2016, Mr. Nayyar filed a
requisition scheduling a judicial management conference with me under the now-completed

Execution Proceedings
. The judicial management conference was held on February
12, 2016. During that conference, Mr. Nayyar advised of his intention to
file a new action. The Nayyars filed their present claim on February 22, 2016
(the “New Claim”).

The Application to Strike

[
36
]

The applicant defendants seek to strike the New
Claim under
Rules
9-5(1)(a) and (d). The applicants also, in their materials,
argue that the claim is frivolous and vexatious. That assertion is addressed in
R. 9-5(1)(b). These various provisions state:

(
1)        At any stage of a proceeding, the court may order to be
struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition or other
document on the ground that

(a)      it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case
may be,

(b)      it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

…

(d)      it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
37
]

In
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2015 BCSC 392
, I
addressed the differences between the various subparagraphs of R. 9-5(1) and
said:

[57]      The test on an application to
strike an action under R. 9-5(1)(a), on the basis the pleadings do not disclose
a cause of action, is whether it is plain and obvious the claim cannot succeed.
It requires a conclusion that, assuming that the facts as stated are true,
those facts disclose no cause of action and the pleadings disclose no arguable
issue. If there is a chance that the action may succeed, then the action should
be allowed to proceed;
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at
980;
Thompson v. Webber
,
2010 BCCA 308
at para.
11
;
Canadian Bar
Assn. v. British Columbia
,
2008 BCCA 92
at para.
37
.

[58]

The test for striking a pleading under R. 9-5(1)(b), on the basis
that it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, was recently
summarized in
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
, where Fisher J. said:

[20]      Under
Rule 9-5(1)(b), a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action, if it does not advance any claim
known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it
would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the court’s time and
public resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish
Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
[1999] BCJ No. 2160 (SC)
;
Skender v Farley
,
2007 BCCA
629
. If a pleading is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is
pleaded, it may also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious.

…

[60]

The abuse of process standard under R. 9-5(1)(d) derives from a
flexible doctrine. It allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where
to do so would violate principles of judicial economy, consistency, finality
and the integrity of the administration of justice;
Toronto (City) v.
C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at paras.
35-37
.

[61]

Though subsections (a)-(d) of R. 9-5(1) address different concerns
and different wrongs, there is also some overlap between these subsections.
Thus, for example, a pleading that discloses no cause of action, contrary to R.
9-5(1)(a), can also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious within the meaning
of R. 9-5(1)(b); see e.g.
Virk v. Brar
,
2012 BCSC 1004
at paras.
69-70
.

[62]

A pleading can be embarrassing if it does not state the real issue
in an intelligible form. It can also be embarrassing if it is prolix, includes
irrelevant facts, argument or evidence. It can be prejudicial if it is designed
to or has the effect of confusing the defendant, making it difficult, if not
impossible, to answer;
Virk
at para.
75
.

[63]

These same concerns can constitute an abuse of the court if a
litigant has been expressly told that there are aspects of its pleadings that
are deficient or defective, and if that litigant persists, in its amended
claim, to advance the same claims or issues in the same way.

[
38
]

In
Gateway Building Management Ltd. v. Manjit
Singh Randhawa
,
2013 BCSC 350
, Burnyeat J. said:

[17]

In
Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union
,
2006 BCSC 750
, Garson J.,
as she then was, provided the following summary of Rule 9‑5
jurisprudence:

In summary, a
pleading will be struck out if:

(a)        the pleadings
are unintelligible, confusing and difficult to understand (
Citizens for
Foreign aid Reform
, [
Citizens of Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian
Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.) ]);

(b)        the pleadings
do not establish a cause of action and do not advance a claim known in law (
Citizens
for Foreign aid Reform
,
supra
);

(c)        the pleadings
are without substance in that they are groundless, fanciful and trifle with the
Court's time (
Borsato v. Basra
, [
2000 BCSC 28 (CanLII)
, [2000] B.C.J. No. 84 (S.C.)])

(d)        the pleadings
are not bona fides, are oppressive and are designed to cause the Defendants
anxiety, trouble and expense (
Borsato v. Basra
,
supra
);

(e)        the action is
brought for an improper purpose, particularly the harassment and oppression of
the Defendants (
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
,
2002 BCSC 466
).

(at para. 17)

[18]

Pursuant to Rule 9‑5, pleadings that are so prolix and
confusing that it is difficult, if not impossible, to understand the case to be
met should also be struck out:
The Owners, Strata Plan LMS3259 v. Sze Hang
Holding Inc.
,
2009 BCSC 473
, at para.
36
.

[
39
]

The overlap that exists conceptually between
Rules

9-5(1)(a)(b) and (d) has particular relevance in this case. The New Claim is
almost incomprehensible. The pleading refers to Rules, to statutes, and to
cases that have no relationship to each other or to the relationship between
the plaintiffs and Costco and/or Manulife.

[
40
]

Thus, by way of illustration, the Nayyars rely,
in part, on an alleged breach of
ss. 118
and
166
of the
Insurance Companies
Act
, S.C.1991, c. 47. That statute regulates the federal
qualifications of insurers and is irrelevant to any possible claim that the
Nayyars might bring. Section 118 of that statute does not create a cause of
action under which a claim can be sustained. Section 166 of that statute
creates a duty of care for directors of insurance companies to act in good
faith and in the best interests of the insurance company. The Nayyars lack
standing to bring any claim pursuant to
s. 166
.

[
41
]

Similarly, the Nayyars, in what appears to be
their prayer for relief, claim 43 different heads or categories of loss – many
of which have no legal basis.

[
42
]

Furthermore, the language used in the New Claim
is almost unintelligible. A few random paragraphs found under the heading
“Concise Summary of Nature of Claim” makes this apparent.

[9]
Disorder
: Costco and
Manulife erroneously mislead the acting judge an existing known fact, for the
property or real property on November 19, 2014 with regards to the co-ownership
for the Family Home. Court order do not defines that fact other then “except
the reservations, provisos, exceptions and conditions expresses in the original
grant from the Crown.”

Power

v.

Grace,
1932 ONCA I 16 “The trend of the authorities is that a mere lien
or charge on the land, either by a co-tenant or by operation of law, is not
sufficient to sever the joint tenancy; there must be something that amounts to
an alienation of title.”

[10]
Code of conduct
: Error of
law and error of fact occurred based on no proper evidentiary foundation, where
the court was actively involved in investigating the facts (inquisitorial)
while Mr. Nayyar was out of the country, Costco’s ‘petition’ for such
Order for Conduct of Sale - eminent domain-resumption/compulsory acquisition
purposes for the Family Home was granted by his lordship Mr. Justice
Romilly, that was conferred on the judge personally, on November 19, 2014 (the
“November motion”); and the Annu’s approval as to the form of the order was
dispensed with, as well.

In other {25 years) matter
CONF#111810111307 Mr. Justice Romilly stated that “I do not want to use
the words.”

EVIDENCE ACT
Proof of judge's signature

27 A document purporting to bear the
signature of a judge of a court in British Columbia, either in his or her
capacity as a judge or as a
persona designatu
, is admissible in evidence
without proof of the signature, authority or official capacity of the judge
appearing to have signed the document.

[11]
Motto
: COSTCO CODE OF
ETHICS 1. Obey the Law (The Law is irrefutable! Absent a moral imperative to
challenge a law, we must conduct our business in total compliance with the laws
of every community where we do business.)

“We want to emphasize that Costco does not
want to sell your home.”

[
43
]

These same difficulties were apparent in the
Judicial Review Petition, in the response to application filed by Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar
for this application, and in the written submissions that were provided by Mr. Nayyar
to me. A representative portion of those submissions state:

Moving forward, it is reasonable to support
Costco or Mr. Van Ommen's application, because we are the
"right-thinking member of society," the "reasonable
parent," the "reasonable landlord," and the "fair-minded
and informed observer," to avoid abuse of process, 'to mark' that
it is
unnecessary, and, it may prejudice, embarrass the hearing of the proceeding.

...

For that reason, we pray to your lordship
for relief that for this
ad hoc
too the field or unfiled chambers record
along with Affidavit #1 of J. Merrell sworn June 14, 2016 to be sealed in a
manner
with marginal note exception on order of judgement respectively,
the court
may confirm, vary or void the order.

[Bolded and
underlined emphasis in original.]

[
44
]

Counsel for Costco said that he believed, but
was uncertain, that Mr. Nayyar was contesting the sale of the Property
because that sale failed to recognize that he had a one-half interest in the
Property.

[
45
]

Let us assume that this is, in fact, the claim
that Mr. Nayyar seeks to advance. If so, it is not a claim that is
available to him as against Costco and Manulife and it is “plain and obvious”
that the claim must fail.

[
46
]

I start with the report of Registrar Cameron,
filed in the
Execution Proceedings
on May 13, 2014 and confirmed in the order
of Master Taylor on May 27, 2014. That report confirmed that Mrs. Nayyar
was the sole registered owner of the Property. The order confirming the report
was never appealed. Mr. Nayyar was present at both the hearing before
Registrar Cameron and Master Taylor.

[
47
]

Next, Mr. Nayyar’s unregistered interest in
the Property, to the extent it had relevance, existed as between Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar.
It had no relevance against a third party judgment creditor. This is so for
several reasons. First, Mr. Nayyar appears to assert, at para. 6 of
the appendix to the New Claim, that he is not responsible for Mrs. Nayyar’s
debts, and he relies on an unidentified section of the
Family Law Act
, S.B.C.
2011, c. 25 [
FLA
] in support of this proposition.

[
48
]

This is not so. Section 81, which confirms that
“on separation, each spouse has a right to an undivided half-interest in all
family property as a tenant in common” also confirms that spouses “are equally
responsible for family debt” regardless of their respective use or
contribution; see
Remmen v. Remmen
,
2014 BCSC 1552
at para.
22
.  Section
81, however, relies on “separation as a triggering event. “Family debt”, in
turn, is defined at s. 86 of the
FLA
and includes all financial
obligations incurred by a spouse during the period beginning when the
relationship between the spouses begins and ending when the spouses separate.

[
49
]

In addition, any interest that Mr. Nayyar
might have had in the Property is not enforceable as against Costco and/or
Manulife.
Section 103(2)
of the
FLA
confirms that “
Section 29
of the
Land
Title Act
applies to a spouse’s interest in land”. Section 29 of the
Land
Title Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 250 establishes that notwithstanding
express or implied notice, an unregistered interest in land is unenforceable
against a person proposing to place a charge on land or taking a transfer of
land;
Bradshaw v. Stenner
,
2013 BCSC 2051
at paras.
34-38
.

[
50
]

Finally, s. 82 of the
FLA
provides
that nothing in Part 5 of that legislation, which deals with “Property
Division”, “affects the rights and remedies of a spouse’s creditors, guarantors
or assignees in relation to family debt”.

[
51
]

Accordingly, and apart from any other
difficulty, there is no merit or prospect of success for the claim that Mr. Nayyar
wishes to advance.

[
52
]

There are still other difficulties with the New
Claim. Rule 9-5(1)(d) addresses pleadings that are otherwise an “abuse of the
process of the court” and extends to applications to strike a claim, or part of
a claim, on the basis of
res judicata
; see
Lehndorff Management Ltd.
v. L.R.S. Development Enterprises Ltd
. (1980),
1980 CanLII 393 (BC CA)
, 19 B.C.L.R. 59 at 63-64 (C.A.).

[
53
]

To the extent Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar
seek, in the New Claim, to revisit both the various orders made in the
Execution Proceedings and the order of the Court of Appeal made August 31, 2015,
those issues have been fully litigated and decided.

[
54
]

It also seems clear that Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar
are attempting to revisit the Benefits Claim. The “Statement of Facts” in the
New Claim is a mere eight paragraphs long. Nevertheless, the following
paragraphs clearly seek to challenge the Court of Appeal’s decision in relation
to the Benefits Claim:

4.         Costco
terminated [Mrs. Nayyar’s] employment contract, without cause in bad faith and
delegated that ‘causation’ and its fiduciary duty to perform its contractual
duty to Manulife.

5.         Manulife
breached its
ad hoc
fiduciary obligations, following the contractual
duty to Costco; and as a result Manulife breached its fiduciary duty and is in
breach of contract.

6.         Costco,
guided by Manulife, breached its fiduciary obligations, flowing from the
contractual duty to [Mrs. Nayyar], as a result Costco bleached its fiduciary
duty and is in breach of contract; and therefore the effects of such breach on
Nayyars’ to fall automatically into other breaches.

[
55
]

This Court maintains an inherent and residual
discretion to prevent an abuse of process of its administration. The doctrine
of abuse of process is intended to prevent proceedings that are unfair in the
sense that they are contrary to the interests of justice. The doctrine engages
the inherent powers of the court to prevent the misuse of its procedure in a
way that would bring the administration of justice into disrepute;
Toronto
(City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at paras.
35
, 37.

[
56
]

This Court has recognized the flexible nature of
the doctrine of abuse of process. In
Harbuz v. Capital Construction Supplies
Ltd
.,
2013 BCSC 1624
, Gropper J. said:

[43]      The
courts have an inherent discretion to control their process and to prevent an
abuse of process. It is a common law doctrine that is invoked principally to
stay proceedings where to allow them to continue would be oppressive:
Blencoe
v. British Columbia (Human Rights Commission)
,
2000 SCC 44
at para.
116
.
Abuse of process is an adjunct of
res judicata
and it serves the same
purpose, although the focus of this doctrine is less upon the interest of the
parties and more upon the integrity of judicial decision-making. The Supreme
Court of Canada established in
Toronto (City) v. Canadian Union of Public
Employees (C.U.P.E.), Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
that where the requirements of
issue estoppel are not met, the court may nevertheless find that relitigation
of an issue would be an abuse of process (paras. 37 - 38 and 42 - 43). In this
way, the doctrine avoids some of the formal requirements of
res judicata

and offers the court some flexibility in order to control its process:
Roeder
v. Lang Michener Lawrence & Shaw
,
2007 BCCA 152
at para.
21
.

[44]      In
Saskatoon Credit Union Ltd.
v. Central Park Enterprises Ltd.
(1988),
1988 CanLII 2941 (BC SC)
, 22 B.C.L.R. (2d) 89 (S.C.), Chief
Justice McEachern (as he then was) exemplified one way in which the doctrine of
abuse of process can be invoked:

Abuse of process
has also been used in Ontario, to prevent a retrial of issues previously
decided even though the parties or issues were not precisely the same in both
actions, in
Bank of Montreal v. Crosson
(1979),
1979 CanLII 1833 (ON HCJ)
, 96 D.L.R. (3d) 765 (Ont.
H.C.) and
Demeter v. British Pacific Life Insurance Co
(1983),
1983 CanLII 1838 (ON HCJ)
, 150
D.L.R. (3d) 249 (Ont. H.C.), aff'd. (1984),
1984 CanLII 1996 (ON CA)
, 13 D.L.R. (4th) 318 (Ont. C.A.).

Many authorities are reviewed by Hardinge,
L.J.S.C. in
Bank of B.C. v. Singh
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2577 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 256
(B.C.S.C.) who based his decision against allowing a fresh action to proceed
against parties to the former action on the ground of issue estoppel and on the
ground of abuse of process against defendants who were not parties to the
former proceedings.

[
57
]

In
Sahyoun
at para.
144
, I said:

Striking a
pleading under R. 9-5(1) is a draconian remedy that is only granted in
egregious circumstances. With that said, it plays a central role in ensuring
that parties comply with the
Rules
, and it provides the court with a
necessary mechanism to ensure such compliance. Absent access to R. 9-5(1), the
court’s ability to control the content and form of pleadings is diminished, the
broader objects of the
Rules
such as efficiency, timeliness, and
cost-effectiveness are undermined, and considerable unfairness may be imposed
on opposing litigants.

[
58
]

I consider that these various considerations are
engaged in this case. The New Claim is incoherent. That deficiency is not or
would not, however, be saved by allowing the plaintiffs to redraft the New
Claim because the various deficiencies in that pleading are much more profound
and fundamental in nature.

[
59
]

The New Claim simply fails to advance any
reasonable cause of action that is relevant to the relationship of the parties
and that has not already been determined on one or more occasions. Furthermore,
the original claim filed by Mrs. Nayyar, in the Benefits Claim, was filed
in 2004, or more than a decade ago. Each aspect of the Benefits Claim has been
appealed and conclusively determined. The same is true of the Execution
Proceedings. To the extent that the New Claim seeks to revisit or re-argue
these same issues, it is both vexatious and an abuse of the court’s process.

[
60
]

Having regard to these various considerations, I
am satisfied that the whole of the New Claim should be struck under R. 9-5(1).

The Application to have Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar
Declared Vexatious Litigants

[
61
]

Section 18
of the
Supreme Court Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 443 provides:

If, on
application by any person, the court is satisfied that a person has habitually,
persistently and without reasonable grounds, instituted vexatious legal
proceedings in the Supreme Court or in the Provincial Court against the same or
different persons, the court may, after hearing that person or giving him or
her an opportunity to be heard, order that a legal proceeding must not, without
leave of the court, be instituted by that person in any court.

[
62
]

The following non-exhaustive factors, identified
by Henry J. in
Re Lang Michener et al. and Fabian et al.
(1987), ),
1987 CanLII 172 (ON HCJ)
, 59
O.R. (2d) 353 at 358-359 (H.C.J.) [
Fabian
], are regularly relied on in
applications that are brought to declare a person a vexatious litigant:

(a)        the
bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue which has already been
determined by a court of competent jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious
proceeding;

(b)        where it
is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no
possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain
relief, the action is vexatious;

(c)        vexatious
actions include those brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment
and oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for
purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)        it is a
general characteristic of vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised
tend to be rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated and
supplemented, often with actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for
or against the litigant in earlier proceedings;

(e)        in determining
whether proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of
the matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of action;

(f)        the
failure of the person instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of
unsuccessful proceedings is one factor to be considered in determining whether
proceedings are vexatious;

(g)        the
respondent's conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial
decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal proceedings.

[
63
]

Fabian
, and the
considerations that are referenced in that decision, have recently been
affirmed by the Court of Appeal of this province in
Harrison v. British
Columbia (Ministry of Attorney General)
,
2016 BCCA 210
at para.
15
and
in
Pearlman v. Insurance Corporation of British Columbia
,
2010 BCCA 362

at para.
5
., leave to appeal ref’d [2011] S.C.C.A. No. 39

[
64
]

Virtually all of the hallmarks of a vexatious
litigant are present in this case. While Mrs. Nayyar may have originally
advanced the Benefits Claim in good faith, that time has long since passed. The
New Action is the fourth proceeding in which the Nayyars seek to challenge the
outcomes of the Benefits Claim and/or the Execution Proceeding. It is clear and
obvious that the Nayyars cannot, at this point, successfully challenge the
various earlier determinations that I have referenced. Indeed, the Nayyars have
expressly been told this by both this Court and the Court of Appeal.

[
65
]

Justice Garson, in her reasons dated August 31,
2015, concluded that Mrs. Nayyar’s conduct was improper and was an attempt
to re-litigate the Court of Appeal’s judgment and it amounted to an abuse of
the court’s process. She made an award of special costs against Mrs. Nayyar.

[
66
]

In the Judicial Review Petition, I told the
Nayyars that there was no merit to the various claims they were seeking to
advance, and that there was no basis for them to continue to challenge the
various rulings that had been made against them. Costco withdrew its
application for special costs only after Mr. Nayyar orally confirmed that
he would not bring any further actions or applications in relation to the same
issues that he had already advanced on behalf of Mrs. Nayyar and
indirectly on his own behalf.

[
67
]

The chronology that I developed earlier in these
reasons identified that several other special costs orders have been made
against Mrs. Nayyar and that Mrs. Nayyar, at her husband’s instance,
had failed to abide by an earlier court order.

[
68
]

Furthermore, the Nayyars have consistently failed,
in the first instance, to pay the costs orders that have been made against
them. It has, instead, been necessary for both Costco and Manulife to enforce or
execute on those costs orders. In addition, at least one such costs order
remains outstanding.

[
69
]

Still further, the pleadings, correspondence,
and written submissions that have been filed by the Nayyars have repeatedly
been rude and sometimes threatening to counsel for Costco and Manulife. These
materials have also stated or suggested that counsel for Costco and Manulife had
been or were acting improperly. A few examples, which are simply intended to be
illustrative, establish this.

[
70
]

In his October 2010 reasons, Walker J. referred
to several manifestly improper emails that Mr. Nayyar had written to
counsel and stated that Mr. Nayyar had “mischaracterized the conduct of
counsel” (
Nayyar
2010 at paras. 9-11, 16).

[
71
]

In oral reasons indexed at
2012 BCSC 1046
,
Walker J. also said:

[10]      I turn now to the matter of costs.
I am satisfied that Ms. Nayyar with the assistance of her husband, Mr. Nayyar,
have continued to engage in a course of conduct to maintain unfounded
allegations of misconduct on the part of defence counsel and their clients in
relation to the application and the drafting of orders.

[11]      Regrettably, those allegations
made their way to the Court file, and as a result the defendants and their
counsel have had to take each of those allegations seriously and to file
appropriate materials so that there can be no suggestion in the record that
they have engaged in any inappropriate conduct. All of this has been to the
defendants’ great expense.

[12]      If this were a situation where the
Nayyars sought to bring a reconsideration application because they genuinely
thought there was a failure to comply with the
Court of Appeal Act
or

Rules
, I would have come to a different view in relation to costs: I would have
ordered costs of this application to the defendants to be set off against Ms. Nayyar’s
entitlement to costs from the judgment following trial. However, in this case,
I am satisfied that Ms. Nayyar’s conduct, facilitated by her husband, Mr. Nayyar,
is conduct worthy of rebuke. There is simply no basis whatsoever for the
allegations that have been levied against the defendants or their counsel.

...

[14]      I am
satisfied that the Nayyars’ conduct is, as I say, worthy of rebuke and should
be sanctioned with an order of special costs payable forthwith in any event of
the cause.

[
72
]

Correspondence by Mr. Nayyar, that was
written on different occasions to counsel, included such statements as:

i)          “You
are lucky you are smiling and laughing with your original teeth...”;

ii)         “...
This is not fiddler or wonderful ventures sweetie this is your karma ... Will
you be in town on Judgment day we will push media to your office or to your residence
I know where you live let me know where you would prefer so I can let them know
to get you both ways ...”;

iii)         “We can
defeat you this very moment ... Do not fan the flames of our anger! There is no
such metal that does not melt in fire! And there is no oath no curse or no blessing
that I cannot violate! You are being a hindrance to worldly well being and to
the course of our destiny. If you do not stop bad practice of law then you shall
surely face consequences!”

[
73
]

The application response filed by Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar
on this application refers to “egregious” and “persistent” conduct by counsel
that is both “immoral” and “abusive”.

[
74
]

Though both Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar have
always been polite in their interactions with me, I have no doubt that my simply
striking the New Action will not deter them in their ongoing efforts to re-argue,
revisit, or re-litigate the same issues that they must, by now, understand are without
any legal merit.

[
75
]

Past history has established that this is so.
The Nayyars reiterated their written demands to Costco within two weeks after
being told by Garson J.A. that there was no basis for their claims and that
their actions were an abuse of process. They filed the Judicial Review Petition
a few weeks thereafter.

[
76
]

After I clearly told Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar
on December 7 and 8, 2015 that there was no merit to any of the various grounds
they had raised in the Judicial Review Petition, and after they told me that
they would not again advance those claims, they wasted no time in doing exactly
that. Mr. Nayyar wrote to Costco and Manulife on December 15, 2015 asking
that they settle his claims with them. On December 21, 2015, he wrote another
such letter. In January 2016, he sought a judicial management conference. In
February 2016, Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar filed the New Claim.

[
77
]

I have repeated this aspect of the chronology to
emphasize the unceasing nature of the Nayyars’ behaviour. Their conduct is
persistent and relentless. They are not receptive to either guidance or admonition
from the courts. They are indifferent to costs orders.

[
78
]

An order declaring that an individual is a
vexatious litigant is a serious matter. It is not an order that is lightly
made. At the same time, that order is, in certain circumstances, in the public
interest and necessary to prevent ongoing abuse of the court’s process.

[
79
]

This is such a case. The Nayyars have been told
repeatedly, and with increasing firmness, that they cannot continue with the
same course of conduct. Such cautions or rebukes have served no purpose. I am
satisfied that it is necessary to declare that Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar are
vexatious litigants.

[
80
]

The fact that earlier proceedings, other than
the New Action, only named Mrs. Nayyar as a party is of no moment. It has
been clear from the outset, and it is clear to me, that it is Mr. Nayyar
who is the directing mind behind these proceedings and that it is Mr. Nayyar who
continues to actively commence or advance these actions.

[
81
]

In such circumstances, courts have been prepared
to declare spouses, who assisted their partners through various proceedings, as
vexatious litigants; see
Daniel v. I.C.B.C. et al
,
2003 BCSC 475
at para.
34

and
Griffith v. Inspector (Retired) Gary House
,
2004 BCSC 1443
at para.
39
.

[
82
]

Accordingly, I declare that each of Mr. and
Mrs. Nayyar is a vexatious litigant. Each of them is precluded from
instituting any legal proceeding against either the defendant, Costco Wholesale
Canada Ltd. or Manufacturers Life Insurance Company, and any related entities,
and their directors, officers, employees, and agents without leave of the
court.

“Voith
J.”
